newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bid hopes, US support ignite Imperial.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bid hopes, US support ignite Imperial.

text.p: Just two days after demerging from parent group Hanson Plc, Imperial Tobacco Plc has seen its share performance ignited by takeover hopes and strong buyer support instead of the expected selling by U.S. investors.
Imperial, Britain's second biggest tobacco company which was hit by news of a court action from cancer victims last week, has confounded such expectations since Tuesday's flotation.

Speculation about a dawn raid helped push up the price to a high of 438 compared with a debut price of 390 pence and the stock was also given a lift by American investor, accounting for some 30 percent of the shares, helding onto their holdings.
The share later traded around 417 on Thursday.

One trader said, "Imperial was always seen as a possible bid target, it was the plum bit of Hanson. We thought 390 pence was a fair opening price, but anything over 400 pence starts to include a bid premium." He added, "Any bidder would have to pay between 500 and 520 pence."

British-based international tobacco firm B.A.T Industries Plc is tipped as a possible buyer, with some analysts citing a strategic fit and saying a deal would help the tax position at B.A.T, which lacks sales in Britain.

"It's not going to go away, just like it hasn't gone away with Zeneca," said one player referring to constant bid hopes for the pharmaceutical company since its split from Imperial Chemical Industries.
But Robert Dyrbus, finance director at Imperial, remained sceptical. He told Reuters, "We've seen nothing unusual in the share activity,"adding he had seen no evidence of a possible bid.
Imperial had been expected to open trading on Tuesday at between 370 and 380 pence per share, but instead opened at 390 and ended its first session ahead at 393 pence.
Dyrbus attributed the share price surge to strong demand in the U.S. after a series of investor roadshows by the Hanson team which visited seven U.S. cities in five days.
"We're just seeing a lot of demand on both sides of the Atlantic. When we started the demerger process we assumed that in the U.S. we would see a sell-off," said Dyrbus.
"But instead investors see us as having all the characteristics of a tobacco stock -- strong cash flow, capital expenditure -- and no exposure to U.S. litigation," he said.
The finance chief said the interest in the U.S. also reflected Imperial's strong committment to export-led growth - a point hammered home in the roadshows.
"Gareth Davis (chief executive) stated he would be disappointed if 25 percent of our activities didn't come from foreign operations by the end of the decade," said Dyrbus.
Last year, just 13 percent of earnings and 15 percent of volumes came from outside Britain.
Davis told Reuters Financial Television export growth could be done with "minimal dilution of margins" adding that expansion overseas would be done in a "very targeted, selected way."
Imperial's concentration of business in Britain has been interpreted as a weakness by some analysts. The market here is seen as fairly mature, with little growth potential left.
The company's bigger rivals have already secured footholds in important emerging markets like China, India and Asia-Pacific countries making it difficult for Imperial to make inroads.
But Dyrbus denied the company was on the back foot in these regions. "We are a late entrant to international markets -- that's certainly true. But we are growing that business.
"These markets are so large that even a small niche presence could have a substantial impact on us."
